title: 401(k) Loan Calculator for Your Maximum Loan and Payment
metaDescription: Use this 401(k) loan calculator to find your largest new loan and payment. Enter your vested balance, existing loans, past loan peak, rate and repayment term.
introText:
With no earlier plan loans, you can borrow up to half your vested balance, capped at $50,000, with a $10,000 floor. Loans you already owe and your highest plan-loan balance in the past 12 months can lower that amount. The calculator subtracts what you owe. It returns the largest new loan allowed and the payment for the amount you want to borrow. Start with Vested account balance, then enter any Plan loans you owe now and your Highest plan-loan balance, last 12 months. Add the Loan amount you want, Interest rate (APR), Term (years), Payments per year and Loan purpose to see the repayment figures and any rule warnings.

In our internal modeling, we applied the loan-limit formula to a $60,000 vested balance with no earlier loans. The limit on all plan loans together was $30,000, leaving $30,000 available for a new loan. For a $10,000 loan at an example 8% annual percentage rate (APR), the payment was $202.76 per month over 5 years. Total interest was $2,165.84, and total repaid was $12,165.84. Those payment figures use a level-payment schedule. They do not establish the rate your plan would charge. Change the inputs below to see how a different loan amount, rate or payment schedule changes the result.

sections.heading: How the Loan Limit Is Calculated
sections.body:
Under [26 U.S.C. 72(p)(2)(A)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/72), the limit on all plan loans together is the smaller of two amounts. The first starts at $50,000 and falls by the amount your highest plan-loan balance in the past 12 months exceeded what you owe today. The second is the greater of half your vested balance or $10,000.

The calculator compares those two amounts, then subtracts Plan loans you owe now to show room for a new loan. That distinction matters when you have borrowed before: the limit on all loans is not the same as the amount you can take out today. Enter the highest balance even if you have since paid down that loan, because the earlier balance can reduce the $50,000 prong.

| Vested balance | Owed now | 12-month peak | Limit on all loans | Room for a new loan |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $15,000 | None | None | $10,000 | $10,000 |
| $60,000 | None | None | $30,000 | $30,000 |
| $100,000 | None | None | $50,000 | $50,000 |
| $200,000 | None | None | $50,000 | $50,000 |
| $200,000 | $10,000 | $20,000 | $40,000 | $30,000 |
| $200,000 | $20,000 | $50,000 | $20,000 | $0 |

The $15,000 balance produces a $10,000 limit because half the vested balance is $7,500 and the statutory floor is higher. At a $100,000 vested balance with nothing owed, half the balance reaches the $50,000 cap. A higher vested balance does not raise that cap: the $200,000 example with no loans also has a $50,000 limit.

The prior-loan example shows why the two subtractions must stay separate. With $10,000 owed and a $20,000 peak, the peak exceeds today's balance by $10,000, reducing the $50,000 prong to $40,000. The calculator then subtracts the $10,000 still owed from the $40,000 limit, leaving $30,000 for a new loan.

Subtracting the $10,000 a second time would count it twice and wrongly leave $20,000 of room. In the last table row, the peak reduces that prong to $20,000, which equals the amount already owed. The result is no room for another loan under the federal cap, even though the vested balance is higher.

sections.heading: Repayment Rules the Calculator Checks
sections.body:
A general-purpose plan loan must be repayable within 5 years under [26 U.S.C. 72(p)(2)(B) and (C)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/72). The statute makes an exception for a loan used to buy a dwelling that will become the participant's main home within a reasonable time. It also requires substantially level payments at least quarterly.

Choose General purpose or Buy a main home under Loan purpose so the calculator can check the term you entered. It warns when a general-purpose term exceeds 5 years or when Payments per year is less often than quarterly. A green note means the entered amount, term and payment frequency fit the federal rules the calculator checks. It does not mean your plan offers loans.

The calculator also warns when Loan amount you want exceeds Largest new loan allowed. Under [26 U.S.C. 72(p)(1)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/72), the portion outside the qualifying loan rules is treated as a distribution. Use the [401(k) early withdrawal calculator](/retirement/401k-early-withdrawal-calculator/) for a tax estimate rather than treating that excess as an ordinary loan payment.

For payments, the calculator divides APR by Payments per year to get the periodic rate. It multiplies Term (years) by Payments per year to get the number of payments, then applies payment = P x r / (1 - (1 + r)^-n). Each payment covers that period's interest. The remainder reduces the loan balance.

| Example rate | Monthly payment on $10,000 | Term | Total interest |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6% | $193.33 | 5 years | $1,599.68 |
| 8% | $202.76 | 5 years | $2,165.84 |
| 10% | $212.47 | 5 years | $2,748.23 |

These rates are examples to replace with the rate in your plan terms. Payment frequency changes the schedule too: at an example 8%, the same $10,000 loan over 5 years has 20 quarterly payments of $611.57 each. At that rate, paying every two weeks produces 130 payments of $93.45 each.

A longer permitted main-home term can lower each payment while increasing total interest in the supplied example. A $30,000 loan at an example 8% costs $608.29 per month over 5 years, with $6,497.51 in total interest. Over 15 years, the main-home example costs $286.70 per month, with $21,605.21 in total interest.

Run your own amount and rate before relying on any example payment. The federal limit and repayment rules determine whether the amount qualifies as a loan rather than a distribution, while the plan document decides whether borrowing is available at all. If the plan document has no loan provision, this calculator cannot make a loan available.

sections.heading: Borrowing From a Solo 401(k)
sections.body: The same federal loan-limit formula applies to an owner-only 401(k), so a solo 401k loan calculator needs no separate limit setting. The plan document must provide for loans, and a provision alone does not establish that a participant loan avoids a prohibited transaction under [26 U.S.C. 4975(d)(1)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/4975). An owner is generally a key employee under [26 U.S.C. 416(i)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/416), so interest on the owner's own plan loan is not deductible under 72(p)(3). Read the solo section of the [401(k) loan rules guide](/guides/401k-loan-rules/), then enter your vested balance in the calculator above.

commonMistakes: The calculator does not include plan fees or determine your plan's interest rate or loan limits. Enter the interest rate and loan amount you want in the calculator.

The calculator does not estimate income tax or additional tax if a loan is treated as a distribution. Use the [401(k) early withdrawal calculator](/retirement/401k-early-withdrawal-calculator/) for a tax estimate, and ask a tax professional about a missed payment.

The calculator assigns no market return to money while it is out of the plan and does not determine where repayments are credited. Account for the borrowed money's time out of the market separately. Whether interest you repay is credited to your account depends on the plan document.
The calculator does not compare a plan loan with another borrowing source. Use [401(k) loan vs HELOC](/compare/401k-loan-vs-heloc/) to compare the borrowing choices.

faqs.question: How are 401k loan amounts calculated?
faqs.answer: The federal limit on all your plan loans is the smaller of a reduced $50,000 cap or the greater of half your vested balance and $10,000. The cap falls by any amount your highest plan-loan balance in the past 12 months exceeded what you owe today. Subtract loans you owe now from the resulting limit to find room for a new loan. With $60,000 vested and no earlier loans, the limit and room for a new loan are both $30,000.

faqs.question: How much would a $10,000 401(k) loan cost per month over 5 years?
faqs.answer: A $10,000 loan paid monthly over 5 years costs $202.76 per month at an example 8% APR. At example rates of 6% and 10%, the payments are $193.33 and $212.47 per month, respectively. These are example rates. A plan sets its own rate. Enter the interest rate from your plan terms in this calculator to see your own payment.

faqs.question: How many 401(k) loans can you have at once?
faqs.answer: The federal loan-limit text states no maximum number of simultaneous plan loans. It counts every outstanding plan loan toward the limit. Your plan document decides whether loans are available and whether it limits their number. Enter all Plan loans you owe now to calculate the room left for another loan.

faqs.question: Can I take a loan from a solo 401(k)?
faqs.answer: A solo 401(k) can provide for participant loans, but its plan document must allow them. The same federal loan-limit formula applies to an owner-only plan, and a plan provision alone does not settle the prohibited-transaction requirements. Read the solo section of the [401(k) loan rules guide](/guides/401k-loan-rules/) before using the calculator for a proposed loan.

faqs.question: What happens if I do not repay a 401(k) loan?
faqs.answer: A plan loan that fails to meet the qualifying loan rules can be treated as a distribution under 26 U.S.C. 72(p)(1). The calculator does not determine the tax consequences of a missed payment. Ask a tax professional to confirm those consequences, and use the [401(k) early withdrawal calculator](/retirement/401k-early-withdrawal-calculator/) for a tax estimate. Your plan document determines whether loans are offered, the interest rate, fees and any limit on the number of loans.
